before: The Nellie, a cruising yawl, turned on her anchor, her sails never stirring, and came to rest. The incoming tide had reached its height, and the wind had almost died. Since we were heading downriver, we could only anchor there and wait for the tide to turn.
after: The Nellie, a cruising yawl, turned on her anchor, her sails never stirring, and came to rest. The flood tide had begun to flow, and the wind had almost died. Since we were heading downriver, we could only anchor there and wait for the tide to turn.
reason: Flood had made means flood tide began flowing, not reached its height; see Jack Lynch annotated 1902 text and nautical make sense.

before: “All at once a murmur of voices began to swell, accompanied by the tramp of many feet. A caravan had arrived. Beyond the plank wall a fierce confusion of rough voices broke out. Every carrier was talking at once. Through the uproar came the chief agent’s wretched voice, tearfully ‘giving it up’ for perhaps the twentieth time that day.... The accountant got slowly to his feet. ‘What an appalling noise,’ he said. Quietly he crossed to the sick man, inspected him, and came back. ‘He cannot hear it,’ he told me. ‘What! Is he dead?’ I asked in alarm. ‘Not yet,’ he answered, quite undisturbed. He nodded towards the clamour in the yard. ‘When your work depends on making accurate entries, you grow to hate those savages. Hate them to the point of death.’ He considered this for a moment. ‘When you meet Mr. Kurtz,’ he continued, ‘give him my message: everything here’—his eyes went to the deck—‘is entirely satisfactory. I prefer not to write. With our messengers, one never knows who might read a letter at that Central Station.’ His gentle, protruding eyes stayed on me for a moment. ‘Oh, that man will advance a long way, a very long way,’ he resumed. ‘Soon he will be someone of consequence in the Administration. The people at the top—the Council in Europe, you understand—intend it.’
